newsitem.title: USA: US lawmaker favors state bank insurance regulation.
newsitem.headline: US lawmaker favors state bank insurance regulation.

text.p: U.S. House Commerce Committee chairman Thomas Bliley said Tuesday he supports financial reform legislation to provide stronger state insurance regulation of national banks.

A reform bill narrowly approved by the House Banking Committee on Friday would allow federal bank regulators to overrule state insurance regulations in some instances. Insurance companies have complained that the provision will lead to unfair and less stringent regulation of bank insurance sales.

"It is an unfortunate result of the different systems of regulation that the playing field is so imbalanced," Bliley, Republican of Virginia, said in a statement. "Fortunately, it is a balance that Congress can corrrect.

The reform legislation would allow banks, insurance companies and securities firms to combine, and also would allow commercial companies to own small banks. The Commerce Committee historically has jurisdiction over insurance matters and received the reform bill under a sequential referral from the Banking Committee.

"We will begin the process of rebalancing the playing field, allowing better competitive opportunities and strengthened functional regulation for both banks and insurance agents over the next several weeks," Bliley said.
Tuesday, the Commerce Committee's finance subcommittee held a hearing to consider the reform bill's insurance regulation provisions.
Bliley was also sharply critical of existing bank regulations concerning insurance sales as interpreted by the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

"The OCC will give its banks as many extra goodies with as few regulations and consumer protections as it can," Bliley said. "The big box of chocolate that the OCC has been offering up the last few years to its federally chartered banks is insurance powers."

Last year, the U.S. Supreme Court affirmed the OCC's right to preempt state regulations of bank insurance sales that were deemed to interfere significantly with banks exercising their authority to sell insurance.
Only banks or bank branches located in towns of under 5,000 residents are allowed to sell insurance under current law.

The Commerce Committee has not announced its schedule for considering the bank reform bill. Under a typical sequential referral, the committee would have to act within 30 days of formally receiving the legislation from the Banking Committee.

Last week, Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach, Republican of Iowa, said under a "general understanding," the Commerce Committee would act within 30 days. But some on the Commerce Committee are said to want more time and could put off consideration until the fall, congressional staffers said.

Even if the Commerce Committee approves the bill, the legislation's fate remains murky. The Senate has not acted on a companion bill and strong opposition among industry groups has blocked earlier reform efforts several times in the past decade.
